Culture as Strategy

Lesson Lectures · learn

"Culture eats strategy for breakfast." You've heard it. But what is culture, and why does it out-muscle the best-laid plan? In this lesson culture stops being a poster on the wall and becomes a strategic asset you design on purpose: the behaviors you reward, the safety to speak up, and the trust that lets a team actually execute. We'll build the idea from real lectures — tap the cards, the diagrams, and the quizzes as you go.

1 · Two ways to get a culture: default or by design

Every company already has a culture — the only question is whether anyone chose it. Simon Sinek frames the whole subject as a fork in the road. Tap each path 👇

What you get when no one tends it. Leaders only think about culture "after something bad happens" — a scandal, a wave of quitting, a failed hire. The culture forms anyway, just out of accident and whoever shouts loudest.

You start from your why, name the culture you actually want, and then build the skills and incentives to produce it. It's not a one-time launch — Sinek calls it "1% better every day," like parenting: you never become an expert, you just practice.

"you can either have a culture by default or by Design and most people think about cultures most Business Leaders think about culture usually after something bad happens"

— Simon Sinek, "Build a Culture by DESIGN, not DEFAULT" · in your corpus

Jensen Huang, founder of NVIDIA, makes the same point from the builder's chair: once you stop just building products and start building a company, culture becomes the thing you have to "put your arms around" — soft, organic, and impossible to ignore.

"building companies means things that are soft and hard to explain like building a company where the culture what does that mean"

— Jensen Huang, "Building a Company Culture" · in your corpus

2 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

These are the precise terms practitioners and researchers use. Tap a card to flip it.

3 · The core relationship: culture is values plus behavior

Sinek's whole argument compresses into one equation. The reason "integrity" on the wall does nothing is that it's a result, not an action — you can't walk into someone's office and ask for "a little more innovation today, please."

Culture  =  Values (written as verbs)  +  Behavior (you reward)

So you rewrite every value as something a person can do — and then promote the people who do it best. Tap each row to see the translation:

"My favorite definition of culture is culture equals values plus behavior. So values number one needs to be written as verbs. It's not integrity, it's do the right thing."

— Simon Sinek, "Company Culture" · in your corpus

4 · The engine room: psychological safety

Behaviors only show up if people feel safe enough to risk them. Harvard's Amy Edmondson coined the term psychological safety for exactly this — and her research finds it is "mission-critical" in any work that depends on knowledge and judgment.

"psychological safety is a belief that employees have that they can bring their full selves to work it means they can speak up when they see mistakes they can ask for help when they're in over their head"

— Amy Edmondson, "How to build a fearless organisation?" · in your corpus

Why is silence the default? Edmondson's matrix explains the lopsided math. Speaking up benefits everyone — but only later, and uncertainly. Staying silent benefits just you — but right now, with certainty. The brain takes the sure, immediate win. Tap each quadrant:

Sinek adds the practical move: when someone admits "I don't know" or asks for help, reward it out loud — "Yes, more of that, please." And note his subtle distinction: expressing vulnerability with confidence is not the same as being weak.

"I can raise my hand and say I made a mistake or I don't understand... without any fear of humiliation or retribution"

— Simon Sinek, "Cultivating Psychological Safety at Work" · in your corpus

5 · How trust becomes results: Lencioni's pyramid

Patrick Lencioni shows the chain from trust to results as a five-layer pyramid — each layer only works if the one below it is solid. It starts with vulnerability-based trust (not predicting how someone acts, but being able to say "I messed up").

"the fear of conflict is a problem... without trust conflict is manipulation in politics but with trust when people are vulnerable and open with one another... conflict becomes Nothing But The Pursuit Of Truth"

— Patrick Lencioni, "The Five Dysfunctions of a Team" · in your corpus

A golf team is people from different departments who perform separately and just add up their scores. A real team is a basketball team — trading off individual benefit for the collective win. Teamwork, he says, "is not a virtue — it's a choice, a strategic one."

6 · Why this IS strategy, not soft stuff

Edmondson reframes the boardroom: in a volatile world, strategy can't be dictated from the top — it has to be tested in the market. That makes leaders scientists, and scientists need safety to say "we might be wrong."

"the job of the board is to treat strategy as a learning journey to treat strategy as a hypothesis that must continually be tested"

— Amy Edmondson, "How to build a fearless organisation?" · in your corpus

Chris White (TEDxAtlanta) shows the cost of getting it wrong: when people feel unheard, they don't quit loudly — they "check out" invisibly, and disengagement runs at roughly 70% of the workforce. His three moves: unblock communication, become responsive, aim higher.

The "disagree and commit" example. When employees raise an issue leaders don't accept, White points to Jeff Bezos's path: address it head-on — "I know we don't agree here, but will you gamble with me on it?" If the reservoir of trust is deep enough, the team moves forward together and keeps working the issue. That's culture turning disagreement into execution instead of a checkout.

⚠️ The #1 trap: painting values on the wall and calling it culture

Sinek's line is brutal: "if you have to write honesty on the wall, you've got bigger problems." A list of nouns changes nothing because nouns aren't actions. Culture is built by rewarding behaviors and promoting the people who embody them — not by a values poster or a one-day offsite. As Sinek says of trust, it's like the gym: 20 minutes every day, not nine hours once.

7 · Check yourself

According to Sinek, why does writing "Innovation" as a company value on the wall fail to create it?

Right — a value must be written as a verb ("find a new way to solve a problem") so you can incentivize and reward it. Nouns are results, not actions.

In Edmondson's matrix, why is staying silent the default behavior in a meeting?

Correct. Silence protects you now, with certainty; the benefit of voice is shared, delayed, and uncertain — so the brain defaults to silence unless leaders make it safe.

In Lencioni's model, what must exist before a team can have healthy conflict?

Trust is the base of the pyramid. Without it, conflict becomes "manipulation and politics"; with it, conflict becomes the pursuit of truth.

🔎 One subtlety → your bridge to the next module

Notice that culture and strategy aren't rivals despite the famous quote — Edmondson treats culture (psychological safety) as the operating system that lets strategy actually get tested and executed. The natural next question: once people feel safe to speak up, how do you channel that into deliberate change? That's leading organizational change — turning a designed culture into a moving one.

🎯 Your move

Take your team's top three stated values. Rewrite each one as a verb — a specific behavior someone could be caught doing today (e.g., "Customer-first" → "drop what you're doing when a customer is stuck"). Then try Chris White's Monday test: ask five people, "What don't we talk about around here that we really should be talking about?" The silences tell you where your culture is blocked.

📚 From the Canon — Schein, Kotter, the Heaths & Horowitz

The lesson above teaches culture as values + behavior and the safety to live it. Four canon books sharpen the same blade: Schein gives you the X-ray (where culture actually hides), Horowitz the chisel (you build it by what you do), Kotter the roadmap for moving it, and the Heaths the psychology of why people actually shift.

Schein is why "values on the wall" fails: the wall is level 2, but the operating system is level 3 — the assumptions revealed by who got promoted or what survived a crisis.

"if you really want to shift a culture you have to shift the assumptions that underpin everything… if you can't shift assumptions you cannot change culture"

— Mike Clayton, "Edgar Schein's 3 Levels of Organizational Culture" · in your corpus

Horowitz makes that actionable: you reach the assumption layer through visible deeds, because behavior comes first and beliefs follow.

"there may be a gap between espoused values and the actual values that are practiced"

— HR Courses Online, "What is: Schein's 3 levels of culture" · in your corpus

And once you decide to move the culture, both Kotter and the Heaths land on the same lever the lesson already prized — emotion, not data. You win hearts before minds:

"you can't appeal to people with data and facts alone you must also account for how people feel… this step is all about igniting the hearts and minds of your people"

— BigIdeasGrowingMinds, "Kotter's 8-step Change Model: Animated Summary" · in your corpus

⚠️ The canon's shared warning: decay-by-default

All four books admit the same blind spot the corpus surfaces — the silent resignation. A top performer "still delivers, still smiles in meetings but the spark's gone" after too many ignored ideas. Schein's posters can't catch it, Horowitz's shocking rules can't reach it, Kotter's missing short-term wins starve the volunteer army, and the Heaths' bright-spots assume a willing Elephant. Culture degrades on its own; maintenance is the job, not the launch.

Go deeper on sourcing in the canon cluster: Schein on the three levels, Horowitz on what you do, Kotter's eight steps, and the Heaths' Rider/Elephant/Path.

3 ways to create a work culture that brings out the best in employees | Chris White | TEDxAtlanta
TEDx Talks · 12:39 · 1,325,680 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~1,783 words

Do you remember when 20,000 people walked out of Google in protest of unfair and unequal treatment of women at the company? On a single day. The protest was dramatic. It was headline-grabbing. It sent a clear signal. We will no longer check our identities and our values at the workplace door. It was also the exception rather than the rule. Because while brave, certainly brave, the Google employees felt safe enough to organize collectively without fear of reprisals. They felt secure enough that even if they lost their jobs, they'd still probably be highly employable somewhere else. Not everyone has that luxury.

Not everyone feels that way about speaking up at work. Social movement scholars would call the Google walkouts a mobilizing structure. Others mobilize in different ways depending on their context and their cause. In fact, walkouts do happen pretty much every day in the workplace. They're just not normally done with our feet. Instead, they're checkouts. They're invisible walkouts that happen with our hearts and with our hands and with our voices. And let's be honest amongst the TED group here. Pretty much all of us have checked out at some point in our careers, haven't we? When we feel psychologically unsafe or unvalued, we protest quietly, sometimes even silently or subconsciously.

Maybe we stop trying as hard at work. Or maybe we act in ways that subtly undermine leadership or act against the organization's objectives just a little bit. In corporate speak, we become disengaged or actively disengaged. Like 70% of the workforce at a cost of hundreds of billions of dollars a year to the global economy. So, if you're an executive and you want to avoid walkouts or checkouts before they become issues at your organization, there are three things that you can do. First, unblock communication. Walkouts and checkouts happen when we feel that we're not being heard, we're not being respected or considered in the workplace.

And just about all of us have experienced having our ideas shot down or ignored in the workplace. When it happens, we tend to experience it as an identity threat. Some of us respond to that by closing down, shutting off. When we feel that we don't belong or that we're unimportant, our reaction is to stop caring as much about our work and caring as much about the people around us. So, I remember feeling heartbroken when I was a new manager. I just asked a colleague of mine with decades of work experience for a recommendation on a problem that she brought to me. We stood in agonizing silence while she searched for an answer, any answer.

After a long pause, she looked up and said, "I have never been asked what I think at work before." Now, that is tragic and it's all too common. And to avoid this pitfall, we need to continually invite people to speak up at work because making these invitations just a routine part of how we engage with each other in the workplace actually lays really important groundwork that is needed for those times when people have to speak up and have to be heard on issues that are hard for management to hear. Backed into a corner by the scale and the intensity of the protests, Google CEO Sundar Pichai had a choice.

He could choose to respond in a way that would close the door to people acting in line with their values or he could choose to open it wider. Pichai's public response to the protest was not defensive. Instead, he sent an email out to the whole company. He said, "I understand the anger and disappointment that many of you feel. I feel it, too. And I'm fully committed to making progress on an issue that has persisted for far too long in our society and yes, here at Google, too. He informed managers of the planned activities. He reassured protesters that they would have the support that they needed.

But checkouts because they're invisible are even harder to notice and address than a 20,000 person walkout. Instead, managers have to proactively unblock the organization. They need to ask questions. They need to invite input. They need to foster creative conflict. But especially in that fragile moment where people have the courage to challenge us we too need to embrace them for it. But then we need to become responsive because we know, don't we, that it's not enough just to hear people out. Words without action breed cynicism. They leave lay their seeds for future walkouts and checkouts. The Google walkouts were not a first step.

They were a last resort. The Google employees had already spoken to managers and HR and ombuds people. This was an escalation because they felt their issues were not being addressed, they're not being taken seriously. And while Pichai's response was a good one, it was supportive some people continue protesting to this day at Google because they do not feel that sufficient action has followed the supportive words. Now when managers and employee activists are on the same page, then action is a natural next step. But here's the thing we're not always going to agree, are we? Sometimes employee activists will raise issues that managers just don't agree with.

And in that fragile moment, we will determine what kind of culture we will have. Will we engage in dialogue and debate? Can we stay unified even in dissent? Or will we choose to skate over our differences, allow our relationships to become inauthentic, and our identities to become diluted? What will it be? Well, at a minimum, we can try to have dialogue. We can try to resolve our differences and find common ground that even if it's not ideal for any one party, might be acceptable for all. And sometimes though, that is just too hard. The common ground can't be found. And in that difficult place, we have three choices.

First, if we feel we can't live with the resolution, then we can choose to leave the company. We can find employers whose values more closely align with our own. Or second, we can choose to stay with the company. We can compartmentalize, keep doing a good job, and hope for an issue, look for look for a time to address the issue again in the future. Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos is an advocate of a third path. He says, "Let's disagree and commit." Address the issue head on, and he'll ask his team, "Look, I know we don't agree here, but will you gamble with me on it?" And if your reservoir of trust in your relationship is deep enough, you can continue to move forward on the work and agree to keep working on the issue as you go.

Any one of those options is better than the the of checking out, which is a sure-fire path to organizational demise and professional misery. So, finally, aim higher. Doesn't it seem like a low bar just to avoid checkouts and walkouts? Shouldn't we strive for more? We need to invite people to bring their whole selves to work because when everyone can bring their life experiences, we just have so much more to offer. We are more than the sum of our resumes. This is Joanne Bohannon. Joanne is a finance director at Disney Europe. She's also a mother. And her son, Roman, has dyslexia. Did you know that one in 10 people live with dyslexia?

That's a huge population serve, a huge potential market for a company like Disney. So, when Disney announced an internal contest uh for new and impactful business ideas, Joanne just couldn't resist applying. She'd heard about modifications that made it easier for dyslexics to read. Wider uh la wi different, larger fonts, wider spaces between letters, ruler between lines, but these weren't widely available. Could Disney help with that? Because Disney invited Joanne to bring her whole self to work and all of her unique strengths, values, passions, experiences, they can now better serve millions of people with dyslexia.

So, all this sounds good. Unblock communication, become responsive, aim higher. Where do we begin? Well, I'd like to end by offering you a short test. I'd like to you on Monday morning to go back into work, and I'd like you to walk around and after some pleasant chitchat, talk to 10 different people and ask them this question. Hi. What don't we talk about around here that we really should be talking about? You'll probably get one of those awkward silences. And that's okay. If they do pause, then say, "Come to me later. Tell me what you find." If no one has anything, then your organization is probably blocked.

But that's okay. By asking the question, you have signaled openness. Keep going. Keep asking the questions. Ari Weinstock, CEO of Zingerman's, likes to say, "Success doesn't mean we have no problems. It means we have better problems." And my closing wish for you is that you earn better problems by unblocking communication, by becoming responsive. Over time, more and more people will open up and start sharing more of themselves, their ideas, their unique offerings. And over time, you will have a new, better problem. Harnessing that energy and aiming higher. Thank you.
